triage.reason: Recurrent headache with characteristic features and red-flag differential; diagnosis is clinical and highly interview-driven.

demographics: Women are about three times more likely than men to have migraine
Affects roughly 12% of people in the US
More common in people with lower household income and in those with public insurance
Often begins in adolescence or early adulthood and peaks in the 30s

risk_factors.text: Family history of migraine in a first-degree relative
Personal history of depression or anxiety
Sleep disorders, especially insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea

family_history: Migraine in a parent or sibling
History of recurrent headaches in the family
social_history: Irregular sleep schedule or shift work
High stress or recent stressful life events
exposures: Strong smells such as perfume or smoke
Aged cheese, cured meats, MSG, chocolate
risk_medications: Overuse of acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or triptans

chief_complaints.text: The light and noise are killing me
I feel sick to my stomach
I get these headaches over and over

hpi.onset: Gradual over 1–2 hours, often in the early morning or after waking; may be preceded by a prodrome hours earlier
hpi.duration: Untreated attacks last 4–72 hours; treated attacks often resolve within a few hours
hpi.progression: Builds from mild to moderate-severe throbbing pain, plateaus, then slowly fades; may leave a day of feeling drained and foggy afterward
hpi.location: Unilateral in about two-thirds of attacks, often frontotemporal or retro-orbital; can be bilateral, especially in children and in tension-type overlap
hpi.radiation: May spread from one side to the whole head or to the neck and shoulders
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe, typically 6–8/10 at peak; disabling enough to stop usual activities
hpi.timing: Recurrent attacks, often with a predictable pattern such as around menses, after a stressful week, or on weekends; each attack lasts hours to a few days
relieving: Lying down in a dark, quiet room
Taking a triptan or NSAID early in the attack

associated_symptoms.text: Visual aura such as flashing lights, zigzag lines, or blind spots
Tingling or numbness that spreads from the fingers to the face
Trouble finding words during the aura
Prodrome the day before: yawning, food cravings, mood changes, neck stiffness
Postdrome: feeling exhausted, weak, or foggy for up to a day after

pertinent_negatives: Worst headache of my life or thunderclap onset
New weakness or numbness that does not spread gradually
New confusion, trouble speaking, or loss of consciousness
Headache that is worse when lying down or wakes me from sleep
Progressive headache that gets worse every day
Vision loss that does not resolve
Weight loss, night sweats, or cancer history

positives.text: Tingling that spreads slowly over minutes

negatives: Sudden severe headache reaching peak in seconds
New focal weakness or numbness that does not spread
Headache triggered by cough, Valsalva, or sexual activity

positives.text: Blind spots that enlarge and drift
Feeling tired or drained after the attack
Mood changes or irritability before the headache

atypical.how_it_differs: Attacks are often shorter (1–72 hours) and bilateral, and children may present mainly with abdominal pain, vomiting, or vertigo rather than a clear headache.
New onset after age 50 is uncommon and should prompt a search for secondary causes; aura without headache and late-life migraine accompaniments are more frequent.
Migraine often improves in the second and third trimesters, but new headache with aura in pregnancy raises concern for preeclampsia, stroke, or cerebral venous thrombosis.

general.mild: Alert, conversant, prefers a dim quiet room but able to participate in the exam
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, squinting or shielding the eyes from light, lies still with eyes closed, answers in short phrases
general.severe: Distressed, photophobic and phonophobic, nauseated, wants the room dark and silent, reluctant to move the head
general.critical: Not typical for migraine; a patient this ill should prompt reconsideration of a secondary cause

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation, attention, and ability to follow commands
findings.finding: Alert and oriented with normal attention and language

findings.maneuver: Test cranial nerves II through XII, including visual fields, pupils, and extraocular movements
findings.finding: Intact cranial nerve function with no field cut, ptosis, or ophthalmoplegia

findings.maneuver: Test strength in all four limbs
findings.finding: Full symmetric strength without focal weakness

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick in the face and limbs
findings.finding: Symmetric sensation without a persistent focal deficit

findings.maneuver: Check deep tendon reflexes and, when indicated, the plantar response
Perform fundoscopy when the history is atypical or red flags are present
Ask the patient to flex the neck toward the chest
findings.finding: Full, painless neck flexion without meningismus

findings.maneuver: Palpate and percuss the frontal and maxillary sinuses
Palpate the temporal arteries in patients over 50 with new headache
findings.finding: Non-tender, non-nodular temporal arteries with normal pulsations

findings.maneuver: Palpate the temporalis and masseter muscles and the temporomandibular joint
findings.finding: No focal muscle or joint tenderness

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms when a secondary cause is considered
findings.finding: No marked hypertension and no arm-to-arm difference

findings.maneuver: Assess cervical range of motion and palpate the paraspinal muscles
findings.finding: No marked restriction or focal spinal tenderness

imaging.study: MRI brain without and with IV contrast

findings.text: Normal brain parenchyma without mass, edema, or abnormal enhancement
Nonspecific white matter hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR
Enhancing lesion, mass effect, or leptomeningeal enhancement suggesting a secondary cause

imaging.preferred_when: Emergency setting when a secondary cause must be excluded quickly or MRI is unavailable

findings.text: No acute hemorrhage, mass, or midline shift
Acute hemorrhage or mass lesion suggesting a secondary cause

imaging.study: CT angiography or MR angiography of the head and neck
imaging.preferred_when: Thunderclap onset, suspected vascular cause, or focal neurologic deficit

findings.text: No aneurysm, dissection, or large-vessel occlusion
Vascular abnormality such as aneurysm or dissection
Patent dural venous sinuses without filling defect
Venous sinus filling defect suggesting thrombosis

initial.only_if: new headache after age 50 with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or visual symptoms

criteria.name: Migraine without aura
criteria.summary: At least five attacks lasting 4–72 hours with at least two of: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate or severe intensity, aggravation by routine physical activity; plus at least one of nausea or vomiting, or both photophobia and phonophobia; and no better explanation by another diagnosis.
items: Attacks last 4–72 hours untreated or unsuccessfully treated
At least two of: unilateral, pulsating, moderate or severe, aggravated by activity
At least one of: nausea or vomiting, or both photophobia and phonophobia
Not better accounted for by another diagnosis

criteria.name: Migraine with aura
criteria.summary: At least two attacks with fully reversible aura symptoms that develop gradually over at least five minutes, last five to sixty minutes, include at least one unilateral, positive, or visual symptom, are followed by headache within sixty minutes, and are not better explained by another diagnosis.
items: Gradual development over at least five minutes
Aura symptoms last five to sixty minutes
At least one aura symptom is unilateral, positive, or visual
Headache follows aura within sixty minutes
Not better accounted for by another diagnosis

differential.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Severe headache is the cardinal feature of both, and a patient with a first severe headache may be unable to distinguish it from a migraine attack.
differential.trigger: Thunderclap headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds to a minute, or a headache that is clearly the worst of the patient's life

history: Sudden onset reaching peak intensity in seconds to a minute
Worst headache of my life
Vomiting at onset
Brief loss of consciousness or a sentinel headache days earlier
No prior recurrent headache pattern
exam: Neck stiffness or meningismus
Altered mental status
Focal neurologic deficit such as third nerve palsy
Fundoscopy showing subhyaloid or vitreous hemorrhage
labs: No specific blood test confirms it; a normal CBC and coagulation panel do not exclude it
imaging: Noncontrast CT head showing subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns or sulci
CT or MR angiography showing an aneurysm
Xanthochromia on lumbar puncture if CT is negative and suspicion remains

differential.name: Meningitis
differential.why_considered: Headache with nausea, vomiting, and light sensitivity is common to both, and meningitis can present without the classic rash.
differential.trigger: Fever with headache, neck stiffness, or altered mental status

history: Fever and chills
Rapid progression over hours
Neck stiffness
Recent ear or sinus infection, or a known immunocompromised state
exam: Nuchal rigidity and a positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign
Fever
Altered mental status or photophobia that is constant rather than episodic
Petechial or purpuric rash
labs: Elevated white blood cell count and inflammatory markers
CSF with elevated white cells, elevated protein, and low glucose
Positive CSF Gram stain or culture
imaging: CT head before lumbar puncture if there are focal deficits or altered mental status; often normal
MRI showing meningeal enhancement in some cases

differential.name: Ischemic stroke
differential.why_considered: Migraine with aura can produce transient focal neurologic symptoms, and stroke can present with headache and a focal deficit.
differential.trigger: Sudden focal weakness, numbness, or speech difficulty that does not spread gradually over minutes

history: Abrupt onset of a fixed focal deficit
Symptoms are negative phenomena such as weakness or loss of vision rather than positive phenomena like flashing lights
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or atrial fibrillation
No gradual march of symptoms over five to twenty minutes
exam: Persistent focal weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, or visual field cut
Facial droop or dysarthria
Symptoms do not resolve within an hour
labs: Glucose and coagulation studies to assess stroke risk and mimics
imaging: CT head showing a hypodense territory or no acute blood
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging showing restricted diffusion in a vascular territory
CT or MR angiography showing large-vessel occlusion

differential.name: Tension-type headache
differential.why_considered: The most common primary headache and the most frequent alternative diagnosis when headache is bilateral and non-disabling.

history: Bilateral, band-like pressure or tightness rather than throbbing
Mild to moderate intensity that does not stop usual activity
No nausea or vomiting
No worsening with routine physical activity
At most one of photophobia or phonophobia
exam: Normal neurologic exam
Palpable tenderness of the pericranial or neck muscles

differential.name: Cluster headache
differential.why_considered: Another primary headache with severe unilateral pain and autonomic features that can be mistaken for migraine.

history: Excruciating pain centered on one eye or temple
Attacks last fifteen minutes to three hours and occur in clusters, often at night
Restlessness and pacing rather than lying still
Attacks occur daily for weeks then remit
exam: Ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, eyelid edema, conjunctival injection, lacrimation, or nasal congestion during attacks
Normal exam between attacks
imaging: MRI brain and pituitary protocol to exclude a secondary cause when the presentation is atypical

differential.name: Medication overuse headache
differential.why_considered: Frequent use of acute headache medication can transform an episodic migraine into a daily headache, and the two often coexist.

history: Headache on fifteen or more days per month
Regular overuse of acetaminophen, NSAIDs, triptans, or opioids for headache
Headache improves after stopping the offending medication
exam: Normal neurologic exam

differential.name: Giant cell arteritis
differential.why_considered: New headache in an older adult can be the presenting symptom and carries a risk of irreversible vision loss.
differential.trigger: New headache after age 50, especially with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or visual symptoms

history: Age over 50 with new headache
Jaw claudication with chewing
Scalp tenderness when brushing hair
Transient or permanent vision loss
Polymyalgia symptoms such as shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness
exam: Tender, nodular, or pulseless temporal artery
Visual field defect or decreased visual acuity
Normal neurologic exam otherwise
imaging: Temporal artery ultrasound showing a halo sign
MRI or PET showing large-vessel inflammation

differential.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
differential.why_considered: Headache with visual symptoms and light sensitivity in a young woman can mimic migraine.

history: Daily or near-daily headache that is worse lying down or on waking
Transient visual obscurations with position change
Pulsatile tinnitus
Use of tetracyclines, vitamin A derivatives, or recent weight gain
exam: Papilledema on fundoscopy
Enlarged blind spot or sixth nerve palsy
Normal mental status and no focal deficit
labs: Normal CSF composition with elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture
imaging: MRI showing empty sella, flattened posterior globes, or optic nerve sheath distension
MR venography showing transverse sinus stenosis

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Severe headache with nausea, vomiting, and visual disturbance can be mistaken for migraine.

history: Severe eye pain with headache
Blurred vision and halos around lights
Nausea and vomiting
Onset in a dimly lit room or after certain medications
exam: Red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil
Corneal haze and decreased visual acuity
Hard globe on palpation
imaging: Slit-lamp examination showing a shallow anterior chamber and elevated intraocular pressure

differential.name: Sinusitis
differential.why_considered: Facial pressure and headache with nasal symptoms can be confused with migraine, especially when the headache is frontal.

history: Recent upper respiratory infection
Purulent nasal discharge and nasal congestion
Facial pain and pressure worse when bending forward
Fever and anosmia
exam: Tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses
Purulent discharge in the nasal cavity
Normal neurologic exam
imaging: CT of the sinuses showing mucosal thickening or air-fluid levels

severity.mild: Infrequent attacks, one to four headache days per month, moderate pain that responds to an NSAID or acetaminophen, minimal interference with work or school, and no nausea or only mild nausea.
severity.moderate: Attacks several times a month with throbbing unilateral pain, nausea, and light and sound sensitivity, requiring a triptan and sometimes causing missed work or school days.
severity.severe: Frequent or disabling attacks, often eight or more headache days per month, with vomiting, marked photophobia and phonophobia, and inability to function during attacks; may meet criteria for chronic migraine when headache occurs on fifteen or more days per month.
severity.critical: Not a feature of migraine itself; a patient who appears critically ill should be evaluated for a secondary cause such as subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, or stroke.

red_flags.finding: Thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute
red_flags.meaning: Suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage or another vascular emergency and requires urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: Fever with neck stiffness or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Suggests meningitis or encephalitis and requires urgent lumbar puncture and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficit that does not resolve or does not spread gradually
red_flags.meaning: Suggests stroke or a space-occupying lesion rather than migraine aura
Raises concern for giant cell arteritis, mass lesion, or other secondary cause

red_flags.finding: Headache that is worse when lying down or wakes the patient from sleep
red_flags.meaning: Suggests raised intracranial pressure or a posterior fossa lesion

red_flags.finding: Progressive headache that worsens every day over weeks
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a mass lesion, infection, or other secondary cause
Suggests intracranial hemorrhage or post-traumatic complication
Suggests raised intracranial pressure, mass lesion, or venous sinus thrombosis

red_flags.finding: New headache in pregnancy or the postpartum period with aura or neurologic signs
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for preeclampsia, stroke, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

red_flags.finding: History of cancer, HIV, or immunosuppression with new headache
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for central nervous system infection or metastasis

complications.name: Medication overuse headache
clues: Headache on fifteen or more days per month
Regular use of acute headache medication more than two to three days per week
Headache improves after withdrawal of the offending medication

complications.name: Chronic migraine
clues: Headache on fifteen or more days per month for more than three months
At least eight days per month with migraine features
Progressive increase in attack frequency over months

complications.name: Migrainous infarction
clues: Aura symptoms that persist beyond sixty minutes
Focal deficit with corresponding ischemic lesion on diffusion-weighted MRI
Usually occurs in a patient with migraine with aura

complications.name: Status migrainosus
clues: Debilitating attack lasting more than seventy-two hours

complications.name: Persistent aura without infarction
clues: Aura symptoms lasting more than one week
No evidence of infarction on imaging

complications.name: Migraine-associated vertigo
clues: Recurrent spontaneous vertigo lasting minutes to hours
Personal or family history of migraine

special_populations.differences: Attacks are often shorter and bilateral, and children may present with abdominal pain, vomiting, or vertigo rather than a clear headache; the diagnosis is clinical and imaging is reserved for red flags.

New onset after age 50 is uncommon and should prompt evaluation for giant cell arteritis and structural causes; aura without headache and late-life migraine accompaniments are more frequent, and medication interactions are more likely.

Migraine often improves in the second and third trimesters; new headache with aura or neurologic signs in pregnancy or the postpartum period raises concern for preeclampsia, stroke, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and triptans and NSAIDs should be used with caution.
Obesity is associated with higher attack frequency and progression to chronic migraine; weight loss may reduce attack frequency.
Dose adjustment or avoidance of certain preventive and acute medications is needed because of reduced hepatic metabolism.
Dose adjustment or avoidance of certain acute and preventive medications is needed because of reduced renal clearance.

key_questions.question: Tell me about the headache — where is it, and what does it feel like?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral, throbbing or pulsating pain, often frontotemporal or behind the eye

key_questions.question: How long does an attack last if you don't treat it?
key_questions.looking_for: 4 to 72 hours; shorter attacks suggest cluster headache, longer constant pain suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Does the pain get worse when you move around, bend over, or cough?
key_questions.looking_for: Aggravation by routine physical activity, which supports migraine

key_questions.question: How bad is the pain at its worst, and does it stop you from working or studying?
key_questions.looking_for: Moderate to severe, disabling; mild pain that does not limit activity suggests tension-type headache

key_questions.question: Do light, sound, or smells bother you during an attack?
key_questions.looking_for: Both photophobia and phonophobia, which support migraine

key_questions.question: Do you feel sick to your stomach or vomit with the headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea or vomiting; their absence makes migraine less likely

key_questions.question: Do you ever see flashing lights, zigzag lines, or blind spots before the headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Aura that develops gradually over at least five minutes and lasts five to sixty minutes

key_questions.question: Do you notice anything in the day before an attack, like yawning, food cravings, or mood changes?
key_questions.looking_for: A prodrome, which supports migraine

key_questions.question: How often do you get these headaches, and how many days a month do you have any headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Attack frequency and total headache days; fifteen or more days a month suggests chronic migraine or medication overuse

key_questions.question: How often do you take something for the headache, and what do you take?
key_questions.looking_for: Use of acute medication more than two to three days per week, which suggests medication overuse headache

key_questions.question: What seems to bring an attack on — stress, missed meals, poor sleep, hormonal changes, certain foods or drinks?
key_questions.looking_for: Recognized triggers such as stress, skipped meals, sleep disruption, menses, alcohol, or aged cheese

key_questions.question: Does your headache pattern follow your menstrual cycle?
key_questions.looking_for: Attacks around menses, which supports menstrual migraine and affects treatment choice

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family get migraines or bad recurring headaches?
key_questions.looking_for: A first-degree relative with migraine, which is common and supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Have you ever had the worst headache of your life, or one that came on like a thunderclap?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden severe onset reaching peak in seconds, which suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, stiff neck, confusion, or a seizure with this headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of meningitis, encephalitis, or raised intracranial pressure

key_questions.question: Have you had new weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or vision loss that did not go away?
key_questions.looking_for: A fixed focal deficit, which suggests stroke or a structural lesion rather than aura

key_questions.question: Is this a new headache pattern for you, especially if you are over 50?
key_questions.looking_for: New headache after age 50, which raises concern for giant cell arteritis or a mass lesion

key_questions.question: Does the headache wake you from sleep or get worse when you lie down?
key_questions.looking_for: Positional worsening, which suggests raised intracranial pressure or a posterior fossa lesion

key_questions.question: Have you had a head injury, cancer, HIV, or treatment that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that raise concern for hemorrhage, infection, or metastasis

key_questions.question: Do you have depression, anxiety, a sleep disorder, or epilepsy?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbid conditions that are common with migraine and affect treatment

reasoning_points: Recurrent attacks of moderate to severe, often unilateral, throbbing headache lasting 4 to 72 hours
Associated nausea or vomiting, or both photophobia and phonophobia
Aura, when present, develops gradually over at least five minutes, lasts five to sixty minutes, and is fully reversible
A personal or family history of similar recurrent headaches
Normal neurologic examination between and during attacks
Red flags for a secondary headache are absent, so the diagnosis is clinical and imaging is not routine
Alternative diagnoses such as tension-type headache, cluster headache, and medication overuse headache are considered

easy: Young woman with a long history of recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches
Clear nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia with each attack
Attacks triggered by stress, missed meals, or menses and relieved by a dark quiet room
Family history of migraine and a normal neurologic exam
medium: Bilateral headache in a child or adolescent with abdominal pain and vomiting
Migraine with aura that must be distinguished from a transient ischemic attack
Coexisting tension-type headache with a mixed headache pattern
Frequent attacks with daily analgesic use suggesting medication overuse headache
hard: New headache after age 50 requiring evaluation for giant cell arteritis
Aura without headache in an older adult
Headache in pregnancy or the postpartum period raising concern for preeclampsia, stroke, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Atypical features such as positional worsening or a progressive daily pattern that require imaging
Chronic migraine with fifteen or more headache days per month
